**INTERNAL MEMO**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Date:** Friday
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?

We've reached the point where our inference workloads are bumping against the ceiling of the hardware we own, and the natural instinct is to reach for the procurement form. Before we do that, I want to argue for a different sequencing: spend the next quarter measurably improving utilisation of our existing fleet, and only then decide whether the growth justifies new capital. I think this is the right call on cost, on risk, and on what it teaches us about our own demand.

The cost argument is the most obvious one. A serious GPU node is a five-figure commitment before we account for power, cooling, rack space, and the engineering time to integrate and operate it. That money is not free; it's an opportunity cost in the most literal sense. Every dollar we spend on metal we don't fully use is a dollar not spent on the product work that actually differentiates us. And the uncomfortable truth is that our current fleet is nowhere near saturated. Our monitoring shows average GPU utilisation in the 30–40% range, with sharp peaks around batch jobs and long idle stretches overnight. That pattern is not a capacity problem; it's a scheduling problem. If we can lift average utilisation to 60% or better through better queueing, batching, and workload consolidation, we effectively add half a node's worth of capacity for the price of a few weeks of engineering time.

Latency cuts both ways here, and I want to be honest about that. One legitimate argument for more hardware is that headroom is a latency insurance policy. When a box is running near capacity, requests queue, tail latencies balloon, and the p99 numbers that our API consumers actually feel degrade in ways that are hard to predict. If we squeeze utilisation too aggressively, we may trade a comfortable p50 for an ugly p99. This is a real risk, and it's why the utilisation work has to be done with latency budgets in mind, not as a pure throughput exercise. But the flip side is that right now our latency problems are concentrated in specific windows, and smarter batching and priority scheduling would likely improve tail latency during those windows rather than worsen it. We should measure this carefully as we go.

Reliability is the quieter consideration. Adding hardware doesn't just add capacity; it adds failure surface. Every new node is another power supply, another driver stack, another thing to patch at 2 a.m. Our existing fleet has known failure modes and known workarounds. Improving utilisation means deepening our understanding of the systems we already run, which tends to improve operational reliability as a side effect. Buying more hardware before we've fixed our scheduling means replicating our current inefficiency across a larger fleet, and paying for the privilege.

The reversibility argument may be the strongest one. Capital purchases are nearly irreversible in practice. Reselling GPUs recovers only a fraction of cost, and the market moves fast enough that hardware depreciates quickly. Engineering time spent on better scheduling, on the other hand, is largely recoverable: the queueing infrastructure, the batching logic, and the observability we build will remain valuable no matter what we eventually decide about capacity. If demand keeps growing after we've optimised, we'll buy hardware then, with much better data about what we actually need — and we'll be buying into a fleet that runs efficiently from day one. If demand plateaus, we'll have saved ourselves a significant purchase. Either branch is better than buying now and hoping.

I want to acknowledge the uncertainty honestly. My utilisation figures come from coarse monitoring, and it's possible that a meaningful fraction of our "idle" capacity is idle for good reasons — thermal limits, memory fragmentation, or workloads that can't be co-located. It's also possible that an upcoming project will change our demand profile in ways that make current trends irrelevant. If the utilisation work stalls or reveals that our true headroom is small, we should revisit the purchase decision immediately rather than letting sunk effort bias us. I'd propose we set a concrete checkpoint: if by the end of the quarter we haven't lifted average utilisation above 55% with latency budgets intact, we take the hardware proposal back to this group with fresh numbers.

My recommendation, then: no new hardware this quarter. Invest the engineering time in scheduling, batching, and observability. Measure utilisation and tail latency weekly. Reassess with real data. It's the cheaper path, the more reversible one, and the one that leaves us better informed whichever way the demand curve bends.

Happy to discuss at Monday's planning session.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Local AI hardware capacity planning for the next two quarters

We've been asked to decide between two paths: purchasing additional local AI hardware to relieve our capacity crunch, or investing engineering time to improve utilisation of the fleet we already own. After several weeks of measurement and modelling, our recommendation is to pursue utilisation improvements first, with a purchase decision deferred until we have better data. Here is the reasoning.

The starting point is an uncomfortable number: our fleet-wide GPU utilisation sits at roughly 34 percent over a trailing four-week window, and that figure is not an artefact of idle weekends. Even during peak business hours, a meaningful fraction of our cards sit in low-occupancy states — small batch inference jobs, development workloads left resident, and training runs that hold memory they no longer need. The capacity problem we feel day to day is real, but it is substantially a scheduling and allocation problem rather than a raw hardware shortage. Buying more hardware today would mean paying to replicate the inefficiency we already have.

Cost is the most obvious dimension. A meaningful expansion of our local fleet would require a capital outlay in the low six figures once we account for the cards themselves, chassis, power, cooling, and the networking needed to make them useful for distributed workloads. Against that, the utilisation track is mostly engineering time: a proper job queue, memory-aware scheduling, automatic teardown of idle sessions, and better telemetry so we can see waste as it happens. We estimate two engineers for six to eight weeks. Even at fully loaded cost, that is an order of magnitude cheaper than the hardware path, and unlike hardware, the scheduling and observability work is an asset that keeps paying off regardless of how large the fleet eventually becomes.

Latency deserves honest treatment, because it is the strongest argument for buying. Our interactive inference workloads have tail latencies that degrade when the fleet is congested, and users notice. But the causality matters: latency degrades because jobs queue behind under-utilised allocations, not because the silicon is saturated. If we reclaim even half of the wasted capacity, queueing delays should fall without a single new card. There is a risk that aggressive preemption and packing introduce jitter of their own, so we would need to protect latency-sensitive workloads with dedicated partitions — which itself reduces headline utilisation. We should accept that trade-off explicitly rather than discover it in production.

Reliability cuts both ways. More hardware means more components, more thermal load, and more failure surface, though it also provides headroom that lets us survive a node loss without degrading service. Our current fleet has no such cushion; a single GPU node failure during a training run costs days. This is a genuine argument for expansion, and it is the part of the case for buying that we take most seriously. However, better checkpointing and job migration — part of the utilisation work — would recover much of that resilience at far lower cost, and we would then know whether the remaining reliability gap justifies capital.

The opportunity cost of the utilisation path is real and should not be glossed over. Two engineers for two months is time not spent on product features. But the alternative has its own opportunity cost: capital spent on hardware is capital not available for hiring, and hardware depreciates quickly in a market where model architectures and accelerator generations turn over every eighteen months or so. There is also a hidden opportunity cost in buying now — we would lock in our current workload assumptions before the utilisation data tells us what we actually need.

Reversibility is where the two options differ most sharply. Hardware purchases are largely irreversible at our scale; resale values for used accelerators are poor, and the spend cannot be unwound if our needs change. Utilisation work is highly reversible: if a scheduling change hurts, we roll it back. This asymmetry argues strongly for taking the cheap, reversible action first and letting its results inform the expensive, irreversible one.

Our recommendation, then: fund the utilisation programme now, target a fleet utilisation of 55 percent within one quarter, and revisit the purchase decision with real post-improvement data. If utilisation stalls above 60 percent while queues still hurt, the case for buying will be strong and well-evidenced. We acknowledge genuine uncertainty — our utilisation measurements may undercount fragmentation, and engineering estimates of this kind routinely run long. But the direction of the decision is robust to those errors: it would take a very large measurement mistake to make buying first the better bet. We'd like a decision by end of week so the scheduling work can begin alongside the current sprint.

appliance.drafter: model MTP head (dynamic depth up to 7), exact verify, batched speculation for up to 8 sequences
appliance.drafter_revision: fc694b54fb0174e0913e6adf86691ef85a4ead47 (the checkpoint's own MTP head, NVFP4 draft head)
appliance.hardware: 2 x NVIDIA DGX Spark, GB10, 128 GB unified memory per appliance
appliance.kv_cache_layout: BF16 paged KV, 16-token blocks: 12 full-attention layers x 1 KV head per rank x head dim 256 (196,608 B per block across layers, 40,121,597,952 B) + QSA indexer carry at 768 B/token (2,507,599,872 B); the 36 Gated DeltaNet layers keep recurrent state outside the pool (SSM state pool 8 slots 454 MB, MTP intermediates/checkpoints 4,115 MB, prefix-cache snapshot pool 16 slots 909 MB); no prefill-MoE weight duplicate
appliance.loop_steering: on (ATLAS_LOOP_STEER=1): after a content-loop tail the watchdog would cut, the next pick skips the cycle's continuation token, up to 3 times a request; output is unchanged where no loop forms
appliance.moe_backend: Atlas: tensor-core NVFP4 expert units for decode/verify (ATLAS_QWEN4EXP_MOE_TC), q38 NVFP4 GEMMs on the checkpoint planes for prefill; expert parallel across the pair
appliance.prefill: 16K chunks, sequence-parallel across both Sparks, row- and chunk-invariant kernels, several short prompts per forward (also from a cached prefix)
appliance.prefix_caching: on (radix tree with SSM/QSA snapshots and prompt-tail checkpoints; a cache hit gives the same greedy tokens as recomputing)
appliance.scheduler: max-num-seqs 8, 16K prefill chunks, SP prefill, multi-prompt prefill
appliance.speculative_policy: model MTP head; per-request dynamic depth up to 7 from an adaptive ladder; batched speculation for up to 8 sequences (depth > 3 for at most 2); exact verify: same tokens as serial greedy decode
appliance.topology: TP2/EP2, direct ConnectX-7 RoCE link (RDMA pair)
